JAIL: COURT REQUIREMENTS ZOOMING

Building Program Top ’64 County Problem

By JIM GALLAGHER

Hoping to meet the needs of Orange County’s fast - growing government was listed today as county level by County Supervisor William H. Hirstein.

A new county jail and space to keep up with the rocketing requirements of superior and municipal courts are the top items among needed physical facilities, Hirstein said.

Close behind, the supervisor tabbed the need for additional county flood control measures.

“People are moving into areas that are not protected flood control - wise,” Hirstein said. “It is the county’s responsibility to provide the channels. Storm drains are a local responsibility. You can compare it to garbage collection. We furnish the truck. You put the garbage in the cans.”

The press on county physical facilities is compounded by the proclivity of so many area residents to get themselves tossed into jail.

“Even with the industrial farm, which houses about 400 we’re in bad shape for maximum detention facilities,” Hirstein said. “The court situation will be temporarily relieved when the supervisors move out of the Brownstone Building and into the Tancred Building. Three courts can move into the Brownstone.”

Hirstein, who lists health and welfare among his supervisorial committee chairmanships, is hoping for the best this year as far as welfare costs are concerned.

Two new measures will change the existing welfare set-up. One is a variation on the well known Aid to Needy Children law, in which families are subsidized if the father is not living with the family. The program taking effect in February is Aid to Children of the Unemployed, and applicants may qualify if the father is with the family, but has no job.

Another welfare innovation is in Medical Aid to the Aged, where the state formerly required individual counties to foot the full bill for the patient for the first 30 days. Now the state will share the burden from the first day.

“We will be required to educate people on relief who are undereducated,” Hirstein said, “in an effort to make them employable. This sounds like a good idea, but it costs money to hire teachers. And there are lots of people now on the unemployment rolls who already have the skills we’ll be attempting to teach.”

Hirstein said the board is determined to hold the tax line this year close to the current $1.66 rate.

“If you expect industry to locate in your county you must stabilize the tax rate,” the supervisor said. That’s why we are not contemplating any - as you - go construction financing. You can’t load an additional 10 to 12 cents on industry for this type of thing.”

Increased property assessments, the board hopes, will provide the tax base to keep up with continually spiraling costs of county government.

The supervisor predicted little difficulty in adapting to Board Chairman William J. Phillips’ edict that each member would maintain his committee chairmanships for another year. And Hirstein said he wasn’t anxious to rush into the hiring of a county administrative officer, recommended by five consecutive county grand juries.

Supervisors have promoted Finance Chairman David Hitchcock to the newly created post of director of administrative, coordination, but this has been viewed as only a small step toward compliance with the juries’ recommendations.

“You have to walk before you run,” Hirstein said. “We (the supervisors) are devoting full time to our jobs, and I foresee no difficulties. There are no areas that are not being covered.”

The 10 - year board veteran said he predicted 1964 would bring no letup in the county’s population growth.

“I only hope new industry will keep up with it,” he said. He pointed to the rapidly - materializing zoo on the Irvine Ranch and the proposed rapid transit rail line between Disneyland and Knott’s Berry Farm as contributing to the ’64 “new look” in the county.

“There’ll be a lot of changes,” said Hirstein. “I can’t begin to predict all of them. I do know we’ll have our work cut out for us.”

ANAHEIM at a Glance

City planners have spurned three requests for apartment zoning and deferred a fourth pending submission of a new set of plans. A total of nearly 1,000 housing units was involved in the three applications.

The rejected requests included a hotly - disputed 213 - unit development by Arthur, Melvin and Fred Bentin projected for the area just east of Anaheim shopping area. The other two projects were condominiums proposed by Harry Kinkor.

The one project given some encouragement by the planners was the 140 - unit project on the south side of Ball Road just east of Euclid Avenue.

Magnolia District School youngsters soon will be among the thousands coming home with the cry of “Look, Mom, no cavities!” The board agreed this week to accept the offer of a toothpaste manufacturer to provide the district with a complete instructional program in dental hygiene for the young children — at no cost to either the children or the district.

Two New Schools In Design

High school district architects are now working on drawings for Katella High School and Oxford High School, as a result of decisions reached last week at a special meeting of district trustees.

The two schools, both slated to open their doors late in 1965, will cost a total of more than $3.5 million. They will be financed under the combination bond and state loan fund of $25 million recently approved by district voters.

Despite objections of Supt. Paul Cook, the two schools will be designed on two-story floor plans, the first such construction in schools since 1940. The controversy between the ground-level school plan preferred by Cook and the two-story arrangement was a major subject of discussion at the meeting.

Trustees speaking for the two-story arrangement stressed their desire to increase the aesthetic quality of the schools, as well as to make maximum use of the land.

Supt. Cook said he believed it better to disperse the student body over a wider area. He added that if the district used the plans for John F. Kennedy High School for Katella, it would save several months, allowing occupancy by September, 1965, instead of just before Christmas.

The two story plan was adopted, however. According to the trustees, no school in the district will go on double sessions because of the delay.

Katella High School, which will be located on Wagner, between State College Boulevard and Rio Vista, will have a capacity of about 2,200 students. It will be the district’s seventh high school.

The $1,250,000 Oxford Junior High, the district’s thirteenth 7-9th grade institution, will have a capacity of about 1,150 students. It will be located at Grindlay and Orange.

Council Going Ahead On Hiring Key Men

By BOB PERLMAN

While the exact location of Anaheim’s multi-million dollar convention hall is still a closely-guarded secret, it appears almost certain the city is going to have to fight to get the land it wants.

Only “legal details” have kept the city from filing a condemnation action on the property already, according to one well - informed city hall source. These details soon will be ironed out, he added.

City councilmen and staff members have refused to identify the parcel of land the city is seeking for the hall, beyond locating it in the Disneyland area. Any one of a half - dozen parcels of land in the area could furnish a site large enough for the city’s needs.

Meanwhile, City Administrator Keith Murdoch has announced a tentative agreement with Disneyland for the park to furnish up to 1,000 parking places on the Disneyland parking lot for convention hall use except during certain periods when Disneyland attendance is at its peak.

The council apparently is confident that the only uncertainty involved in the land acquisition is the price the city will have to pay. Councilmen Tuesday night agreed to speed up preliminary retention of an architect for the development, as well as hiring a convention hall consultant.

The consultant, who will probably be presently employed as a convention hall manager, will join the council and the architect in determining specifications for the structure. These include square footage of display area and amount of seating in the sports arena.

NEVER TOO EARLY — Tracy Patrick, 5, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Richard Patrick of Anaheim, tells Art McKenzie it’s never too early to get in the habit of dropping a coin in a coin collector, especially if it is a March of Dimes coin collector. McKenzie of Costa Mesa, is the director for the 1964 March of Dimes campaign. Little Tracy, 1964 poster girl who was born with major birth defects, would like to remind everyone who drops a silver coin into the coin collection this January, that it will help to foretell a brighter future and better medical care for the disabled and those stricken with crippling birth defects and arthritis. Tracy, who is now able to walk with the aid of crutches, is receiving care through the March of Dimes.

2—The Anaheim Gazette	Thursday, January 2, 1964
ANAHEIM, CALIFORNIA

CARDINAL’S MASS

St. Boniface Dedication

Church and civic leaders from all over Southern California will attend a dedication service to be held at the St. Boniface Roman Catholic Church, Sunday.

His Eminence Francis O. Cardinal McIntyre will hold a solemn mass at the dedication service at 10:45 a.m. His Eminence will be assisted by St. Boniface Parish’s Rev. John C. Quatmann.

The impressive church structure was begun in December, 1961, and the first mass was observed in July, 1963. Total capacity is 1280. On the facade is a likeness of St. Boniface.

The modern construction shows the progress of the oldest established Roman Catholic church in Anaheim. The previous church on the corner of Harbor and Center Streets will be demolished to furnish playground for the expanding St. Boniface School.

The school now enrolls over 800 children under the direction of Sister Mary David, O.P. Loudspeakers and chairs outside the church will be provided for the anticipated overflow crowd.

‘Y’ Picks Wetzler As Chief

Robert L. Wetzler, commercial developer, was elected to the presidency of the Anaheim YMCA at the December meeting of the Board of Directors (Dec. 16) at the YMCA headquarters.

Wetzler will be formally installed at the 41st Anaheim YMCA annual meeting at the Disneyland Hotel in February and succeeds Richard W. Gay. Anaheim banker, who completes three one - year terms as president. He served in sales promotion in Illinois and during World War II with the U.S. Army combat engineers. He is active in the membership of the First Presbyterian Church of Anaheim and serves on the Orange County Fair Board. He resides at 118 Eisner Street with his family including his wife Ethel, daughters Roberta and Mary and son Tom. He is currently serving as Anaheim YMCA treasurer.

Others elected to the 1964-5 term are Clifford Haskell market executive; vice president of Finance; James Albrecht, school principal, vice president of Program; Mrs. Al Casebeer, housewife, Recording Secretary; and Dr. William Kellogg, dentist, treasurer.

The YMCA board took additional steps toward the construction of a central YMCA facility at the meeting. The organization provides varied youth and adult programs in the Anaheim, Magnolia, Cypress, Stanton, Savanna and Dairyland areas and is an Anaheim United Fund agency.

Real Estate Hike Seen For County

Real estate sales in Orange County during 1964 are expected to show a substantial increase over 1963, according to a poll of selected brokers and builder developers conducted by Santa Ana Savings and Loan Association.

The Orange County opinion sampling, part of a statewide poll conducted by the seven California savings and loan associations affiliated with Great Western Financial Corporation, showed that 85.6 per cent of the respondents believe their sales during the next 12 months will equal or exceed 1963.

Stewart McPherson, president of the association, said 54.3 per cent expect an increase of 10 per cent or more, while 25.7 per cent anticipate gains of 20 per cent or better.

PERSONAL MENTION

JAMES W. DWYER of 1217 Malboro Ave., has joined the Los Angeles Quarter Century Club of Lever Brothers Company.

In recognition of his 25 years of service with the company, Dwyer was presented with a diamond-studded club pin and a $100 U.S. Savings Bond.

The club now has an active membership of 58. It also includes employees from Lever’s sales district in California, Arizona and Colorado.

Six Anaheim students at Orange State College have been nominated for national recognition in the “Who’s Who Among Students in American Universities and Colleges.”

Selections were made by a student committee and were based on scholarship, citizenship, leadership, campus activities and general service and contribution to the college. Students eligible for nominations must be classified as upper-division or graduate at OSC and meet the qualifications of the College.

The students honored were JACK R. CLEMENT, Social Science, graduate; WARREN J. DEACON, language arts major, senior; LLOYD L. FREEBERG, psychology, junior; VICTOR HAUSMINGER, business major, senior; BARBARA A. REES, English, senior; and DONALD A. YONTS JR., history major, senior.

A straight-A average earned a place on the Dean’s List of the University of Southern California’s College of Letters, Arts, and Sciences for SUSAN R. WINER, 132 Guinda Lane, a history major.

Forty-five students were so honored.

Appointment of Maynard Kambak, 2046 Minerva St., to assistant manager of the Fullerton office of United California Bank, has been announced by Frank L. King, chairman of the board.

Kambak was educated in South Dakota. He entered the banking business with the First National Bank of Oberlin in 1957 where he remained until 1962 when he left to come to California. He joined United California Bank in 1963 in its California division, Los Angeles Headquarters, where he remained until his promotion just announced.

Geier Names Gen. Manager While He’s at Political Wars

James A. Hunt of Garden Grove has been appointed general manager of the Orange public relations firm of Robert A. Geier & Associates, according to Bob Geier, head of the firm.

Hunt has been working with the firm on an associate basis for almost a year, specializing in industrial relations and business and political campaigns.

“I expect to devote practically full time to campaign duties and don’t want a repetition of the almost total destruction of the last time I ran for the Congressional seat,” said Geier.

Geier recently announced his intention to seek the 34th District Congressional seat. He was the unsuccessful candidate for the same position in November of 1962, narrowly losing to Congressman Richard Hanna.

Because of Congressional protocol, in view of his candidacy, Geier has resigned as district representative to Rep. James B. Utt, breaking a 12 - year relationship with the veteran legislator from the 35th District.

Bank Names Berry to Audit Post

Thomas C. Berry of Anaheim has been promoted to assistant chief inspector in Bank of America’s audit and inspection department at Los Angeles Headquarters.

His promotion was announced by William J. Breen, vice-president in charge of personnel relations for the bank in Southern California.

In his new post Berry will be responsible for auditing the records of the bank’s administrative departments in Southern California.

In the audit and inspection department since 1958, Berry was promoted to full inspector rank last year. He first joined Bank of America in 1952 as a teller at the Melrose - Irving branch in Hollywood.

A Texan by birth, Berry attended high school in Austin and began his career there at the Capital National Bank.

He has supplemented his professional experience with courses from the American Institute of Banking, educational wing of the American Bankers Association.

U.S. Pact Awarded to Aeronutronic

The U. S. Air Force has awarded a contract for approximately $1-million to Aeronutronic Division of Philco Corporation, to improve techniques to penetrate enemy ICBM defense systems.

Announcement of the contract was made by John B. Lawson, general manager of Aeronutronic and a vice president of Philco Corporation, a Ford Motor Company subsidiary.

Lawson said that the contract calls for Aeronutronic to conduct a study and flight test program for developing advanced techniques designed to overcome possible enemy radar and anti-missile target defenses.

Details of the two-year contract are classified.

Lawson said that the program is assigned to Re-Entry and Space Systems Programs, directed by Charles G. Gant.

Philco’s Aeronutronic Division has been working since mid-1958 on development of penetration aids systems in support of Air Force ICBM programs.

Red Cross Selects Executive

GEORGE W. HAGAN
. . . new director

George W. Hagan is the new Executive Director of the Anaheim Chapter of the American Red Cross. He replaced Miss Gwen O’Neal who served in this capacity the past year.

Hagan has been affiliated with the American Red Cross since March, 1952. In the Korean War he served with the American Red Cross as a field director in the service at military installations, and in 1956 was transferred to the civilian program. He has served as Red Cross field representative in eastern Washington and northern Idaho and also in the same capacity for the state of Oregon.

He comes to Anaheim from the Western Area Office in San Francisco where he has been a member of the Disaster Services Staff for the nine western states. In 1961 he served as administrative director of the Western Area Blood Program and just recently rejoined the National Disaster Staff.

He is a native Californian and holds a Bachelor of Science degree from Oregon State University.

Communication Expert Sets OCC Talk Jan. 15

Dr. S. I. Hayakawa, a specialist in the study of how language and thinking influence human behavior, will appear at Orange Coast College Jan. 15.

Dr. Hayakawa’s lecture, to start at 8 p.m. in the OCC Auditorium, is the second in the school’s 1963-64 Community Arts Series.

A professor of language arts at San Francisco State College, Dr. Hayakawa has held semantics as his major concern since 1937.

He wandered from the field of English into anthropology, sociology, psychology, psychiatry, art and music.

“I could see no reason why a specialist has to be a specialist in one field. At this time, 1937, the most important historical events were the depression and the rise of Hitler and Mussolini. The most impressive thing about Hitler was that he was the first great demagogue and political leader to achieve his position by radio.

Leaders Called to Sacramento As State Heads Off Problems

Southern California leaders in industry, science, government, and education have been invited to be among 500 colleagues throughout the state to meet in Sacramento January 27-28 to launch a sweeping attack on problems confronting California in the next two decades.

Major figures in the state’s civic, professional, and business life will confer about the uses of land, water, and air; problems of food, shelter, transportation, livelihood, and recreation.

Daniel G. Aldrich, Jr., chancellor of the University of California, Irvine, and Charles S. Thomas, Jr., chancellor of the University of California, Irvine, and former president of Trans World Airlines, are among principal speakers on a list which is headed by Governor Edmund G. Brown.

Also speaking at the meeting which will take place at Sacramento’s Hotel El Rancho, are Philip A. Leighton, professor of chemistry, emeritus, Stanford University, James A. Pike, Bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of California, Hale Champion, director of finance, State of California, Edward H. Holmes, director, Office of Planning, Bureau of Public Roads, United States Department of Commerce, W. J. O’Connell, industrial consultant on water problems, Frederic Bold, attorney and Harvey Banks, consulting engineer and former director of the Department of Water Resources, and others.

A panel discussion by six California industrialists will deal with the topic “What Industry Sees in the 1980’s.”

Governor Brown has urged business and government leaders to support the meeting, noting, “It will be the function of this conference to look at some of the problems of growth and see how we can meet them in the years ahead through joint federal, state and local action in a partnership for progress among government, business, and private industry.

“Failure to plan now for the 1980’s will give our children and grandchildren a bitter heritage of a desecrated land.”

Information regarding attendance at the Sacramento meeting may be obtained from the Conference Department, University of California Extension, Berkeley 4.

NEWS OF SOUTHERN COUNTIES

ANNUAL FAIR ON
IN KERN COUNTY

Bakersfield Flooded With
Thousands of Visitors

School Children Throng to
Opening of Affair

Special Program Offered to
Please Youngsters

[EXCLUSIVE DISPATCH]
BAKERSFIELD, Oct. 6.—With
a warm October sun beaming ap-
proval, and thousands of visitors
doing the same, the Kern County
Fair is off to a most auspicious
start. Every department of the
great fair was ready for the in-
spection of the vast throng that be-
gan to pour through the gates at
noon and expressions of surprise
and delight were heard on every
side.

The motorcade of 600 visiting
realty men, from the south, en
route to the State convention at
Fresno, reached the fair grounds
at noon and, after a dinner served
under the giant cottonwood trees
of Lunch Grove, scattered through-
out the grounds for an hour’s in-
spection of the various exhibits.

It was when the 20,000 school
children reached the grounds, fol-
lowing the big parade downtown,
that the huge inclosure took on a
real circus aspect. The youngsters
poured through the numerous ex-
hibit halls and all parts of the
grounds, constantly finding new
things to excite their wonder and
admiration.

This afternoon a program of
racing and vaudeville stunts was
given in front of the grand stand
with special emphasis on events to
please the children.

Late yesterday it was decided to
add a bicycle race to the program
of the afternoon and in a short
while twenty-seven entries were
obtained. Local dealers are donat-
ing prizes for the winners.

The advance guard of out-of-
town visitors began streaming into
the city today and tonight and ap-
parently every road in Kern coun-
ty leads to Bakersfield. Proud of
the exhibits made by their sec-
tions and anxious to see the fair
as a whole, residents from all parts
of the county are here for the big
fair, many of them planning to
stay the entire five days.

PLAN HALLOWEEN FETE

Anaheim Merchants Will Again
Sponsor Gay Carnival

[EXCLUSIVE DISPATCH]
ANAHEIM, Oct. 6.—Preliminary
plans for the annual Hallowe’en
carnival, to be held Friday night,
the 30th inst., under the auspices
of the Merchants’ and Manufac-
turers’ Association, are well under
way, according to announcement
made today by Arthur Cohen, pres-
ident of the association.

Following last year’s custom, the
big event on the Hallowe’en pro-
gram will be the carnival parade,
featuring gaily decorated and
lighted floats, for which prizes will
be awarded. The committee in
charge of floats consists of Cohen
and H. M. V. Barnes. The judges
who will designate prize winners
will be J. A. Claye, chairman;
Mayor Perry W. Mathis, Mrs. Hel-
en Hardin and Mrs. E. E. Smith.

R. B. Young, who will be in
charge of the parade, is making
an effort to have the various
schools of the city represented in
the line of march, with distinc-
tive floats and costumed children.
Prizes also will be awarded for
the best-decorated store windows
in the city.

FILM ACTOR JAILED
AS SPEED SEQUENCE

A regular film chase sequence,
the “sure fire” one of comedy and
thriller, ended yesterday in Police
Judge Richardson’s court when
Russell Land, said to be a film ac-
tor, was given thirty days in jail
on a charge of reckless driving.
Land was declared by Motorcycle
Officer Fetterhoff to have driven
his motorcycle at a terrific speed
for several miles in attempting to
elude the officer. Land lives at
6044 Lexington avenue.

FINED ON POSSESSION
OF LIQUOR AND STILL

Federal Judge Henning yester-
day fined Sam Simmons $250 on
two counts of possessing liquor and
operating a still. Simmons was
taken into custody July 20, last.
The fine was divided into $200 for
operation of the still and $50 for
possession of 300 gallons of liquor.
D. G. Taylor represented the de-
fendant.

Anaheim Proves
Gracious Host
at City’s Frolic

ANAHEIM, Nov. 1.—Merchants of
this city last evening were hosts to
a throng estimated at 35,000 peo-
ple attracted to Anaheim’s fifth an-
nual Halloween Festival. George W.
Reid, secretary of the Merchants
Association and general manager of
the affair, declares the fete the
most successful ever presented here.

Marching and rolling beneath a
bower of gay banners and drapes,
a parade more than a mile long
coursed through the streets, packed
with a seething mass of humanity
bent upon holiday pleasures. There
were no disorders and no accidents
in the city during the evening.

Floats and marchers in the pa-
rade were decorated in the fantastic
and bizarre motif of the day, and
ranged from the sublime to the ri-
diculous. A group of musicians rid-
ing on a colorfully decorated truck
sang and played the airs of the
Spanish dons. Immediately behind
this more sedate entry there was a
group of small boys, some riding,
some pushing the tongueless run-
ning-gear of an old buggy. The boys
were masked, as were many of the
participants in the parade.

Following the parade the crowd
divided into three sections, one to
see a night football game, another
to witness a free vaudeville program
and the third to spend the re-
mainder of the evening at a free
street dance.

Give Land for
Truck Highway

GLENDALE, Nov. 1.—The Los An-
geles Park Commission is ready to
cede fifteen to eighteen acres of
park land as a right of way for the
proposed truck boulevard along the
Los Angeles River to connect San
Fernando Valley with Los Angeles,
Van Griffith, chairman of the com-
mission, told a group of valley
business men meeting here today.
The park commission, Griffith de-
clared, is strongly in favor of mak-
ing the proposed truck boulevard
200 feet wide through Griffith Park,
adding that the proposed highway
would serve more than a purely lo-
cal need and would eventually be
linked up with Ventura Boulevard.

The meeting, held under the aus-
pices of the South Glendale Busi-
ness Men’s Association, adopted a
resolution setting forth the follow-
ing proposed width of the truck
highway: 200 feet between Victory
Boulevard and Los Feliz Road, 140
feet to Glendale avenue, and 100
feet between Glendale avenue and
Dayton avenue in Los Angeles. At
the other end the boulevard would
be 100 feet between Lake street and
San Fernando Road.

HALLOWEEN PRANK
INJURES AUTOISTS

CHINO, Nov. 1.—A heavy bread
box placed squarely in the middle of
the intersection of Edison and Cen-
tral avenues last night by Hallo-
ween roysterers caused two persons
to be sent to San Antonio Commu-
nity Hospital, Upland, with serious
injuries, and two others narrowly
escaped death.

The injured are Mrs. L. A. Gann,
Hollywood, eight broken ribs, brok-
en pelvic bones, right arm and leg
broken, possible internal injuries;
L. A. Gann, her husband, arm brok-
en, three ribs broken, back sprained,
possible internal injuries.

Mr. and Mrs. Gann were return-
ing from a Halloween party to Cor-
ona with B. F. Wooden of Bald-
win Park and S. L. Wooden. B. F.
Wooden was driving a large tour-
ing car. Suddenly he spied the large
bread box directly in the path of
the car and swerved to miss it. The
car left the pavement and turned
over. Two of the Gann children
had requested to ride with friends
in another car just before the acci-
dent and consequently escaped the
accident. Chino police today sought
the boys who had placed the bread
box at the intersection.

AIRPORT SITE OFFERED

SAN FERNANDO, Nov. 1.—An-
other airport site has been offered
to the Los Angeles City Council for
consideration. The site is at Fer-
nangeles on San Fernando Road.
It is parallel to Tujunga Wash and
has facilities for a runway 4000 feet
long and 1000 feet wide. The site is
owned by G. Curtis.

NEW ASYLUM DEDICATED

Grand Lodge Officials Take Part in Ceremonies Held at Glendale Monday Night

GLENDALE, Oct. 8.—Grand Lodge officers of the Knights Templar from all over California assembled last night to take part in the dedication of the asylum of the Glendale Commandery, No. 53, in the Masonic Temple, with Robert Gaylord, Grand Commander for California, in charge of the ceremonies.

Pleasure Trip Is Deferred by Two Burglaries

GLENDALE, Oct. 8.—The visit that Mr. and Mrs. Donald McGregor had planned to make to points in Canada was badly disarranged when two burglaries, occurring within twenty-four hours robbed them of their supply of travelers’ checks and of the money they had obtained to replace the first loss.

The couple had been the guests of Mr. and Mrs. J. M. McGregor at 1276 Boynton avenue and a short time before the hour set for their departure Donald McGregor bought $400 worth of travelers’ checks, which he left in the pocket of a coat hanging in a closet in his room.

The checks vanished, although the railroad tickets were left in the coat. Mrs. J. M. McGregor advanced funds to replace those that had been stolen, and Mrs. Donald McGregor stowed the currency away in her purse. The purse disappeared and when it was found later under a hedge near the house the money was gone. Detective Lieutenant F. C. Williams is working on the case for the local police, and a detective agency has also been retained to investigate the mystery.

Judges Chosen for Apple Show

YUCAIPA, Oct. 8.—Three Redlands women have been chosen to judge canned fruit exhibits at the Yucaipa apple show the 24th to the 27th inst., inclusive. They are Mrs. M. Fitzsimmons, Mrs. W. R. Clyde and Mrs. C. H. Peters.

Rules for this department of the show were announced yesterday by the chairman, Mrs. Otto Sweeters, as follows:

(1.) All fruit entered must be at the show by 10 a.m. the 24th inst.

(2.) First prize of two dozen quart jars for best quart of fruit and also for the best quart of vegetables.

(3.) Second prize of one dozen quart jars for best quart of fruit and also for the best quart of vegetables.

(4.) The fruit remains the property of the exhibitor and any number of quarts of fruit of vegetables may be entered by any exhibitor. Any one in the valley may enter for competition.

The prizes for the competition have been donated by the Kerr Jar Company. The exhibit will be separate from the regular canned fruit booth of the Woman’s Club where fruit and jellies will be for sale.

GIRL STUDENTS IN DRIVE FOR FUNDS

REDLANDS, Oct. 8.—Girls of Redlands High School have pledged to raise $225 for the Mabel B. Woodbury scholarship fund and are now making plans for sales to get the money. Each class has a chairman and those selected to direct the work are: Claire Clark, senior; Nancy Hoover, junior; Ruth Annibell, sophomore, and the subchairmen are: Senior, Irene Dostal, Jean Sanford, Beatrice Maser, Beth Atchison, Chrystal Caldwell, junior, Leona Arth, Jane Brannum, Marcia Cafer, Evelyn Dibble, Ruth Dickerson, Kathryn Lewis, Charlotte Muscart, Edna Nowell, Josephine Reay, Doris Burns; sophomore, Met Jackson, Lucille Tanner, Elizabeth Hatfield, Christy McCarty, Kathryn Walker, Sayako Miki, Helen Ary and Lillian Rigby.

MINT CANYON PHONE LINE TO BE EXTENDED

NEWHALL, Oct. 8.—Plans for the construction of nine miles of pole lines and the placing of 14,000 feet of telephone cable in Mint Canyon, at a cost of about $7100, have been completed by the Pacific Telephone Company. The new lines will give service to subscribers residing in the canyon. All work will be finished by the early part of next year it is stated.

William McMillan, Commander of the Glendale Commandery, introduced the visiting officials and seventeen past commanders of the local organization.

Gaylord and Chief Justice Waste of the State Supreme Court were the principal speakers. The past grand commanders who attended were: Judge Benjamin F. Bledsoe of Los Angeles, Albert E. Boynton of San Francisco, Perry W. Weidner of Los Angeles, Charles Malcolm of Long Beach, Charles Day of Hollywood, Past Grand Commander of Indiana; George Burnham of San Diego, Andrew J. Copp, Jr., of Los Angeles, Robert Wankowski of Culver City.

Officers Find Case of Drugs in Santa Paula

SANTA PAULA, Oct. 8.—A case of marihuana containing fifty-seven tins of the drug, a barrel of imported china and a trunk of silks were taken from the house on Ojai street, here, occupied by Helen Nava, her husband and Manuel Carsino, in a raid conducted there last night by Chief of Police Thornton Edwards of Santa Paula, Officer Burns and Deputy Sheriffs Fraser and Hearne.

The raid of the Nava home was instigated in an effort to locate two guns believed stolen from a local section house.

The officers surprised the occupants about 2 o’clock this morning and in looking for the guns came upon the marihuana. As Chief Edwards stopped to pick up the case Nava succeeded in getting away, the officers said. They added that Nava had very little, if any, attire at that moment.

While the search was in progress a taxi drew up and when Joe Gonzales, the driver, entered the house he, too, was placed under arrest. The two men and one woman are being held pending further investigation.

Gravel Truck in Wild Dive

GLENDALE, Oct. 8.—A truck loaded with gravel while descending the steep grade on La Crescenta avenue, near Verdugo City, today became unmanageable when the drive shaft broke and the brakes burned out, and plunged into a vineyard, scattering its load over about an acre of ground and coming to a halt with its nose buried among the vines and with its rear wheels high in the air. The driver kept on going and when Sergt. Evans of the motorcycle squad arrived at the vineyard he was out of sight.

The accident attracted a crowd of curious spectators, and while they were watching the work around the truck four cars collided. None of the occupants was injured.

SOUTHERN COLLEGES FORM ORGANIZATION

REDLANDS, Oct. 7.—Meeting to form a Pacific Southwest Sociological Association, representatives from eight colleges gathered at the Windsor Tea Room in Los Angeles Saturday afternoon, October 5.

Election of officers resulted with Prof. E. S. Bogadus of University of Southern California sociology department, president; Prof. William Kirk of the sociology department of Pomona, vice-president; and Prof. Osborn, University of Redlands sociology department, secretary and treasurer. The executive committee will be composed of these three officers.

According to plans made during Saturday’s meeting, the association will meet jointly with the Southwest Pacific Academy of Social Sciences in January. In addition to this meeting, the association will hold individual meetings every six months.

Colleges represented in the association are: Pomona, University of Southern California, University of Redlands, Whittier College, Occidental College, Pasadena Junior College, Fullerton Junior College and California Christian College.

SAN DIEGO, Oct. 8.—Charges of Stanley Gee, State Labor Commissioner, that contractors working on the new addition to the Jefferson school have violated the State labor law providing for an eight-hour day on public works, will be reviewed by the Board of Education on the 12th inst., according to a decision made at a meeting of the board.

SALVATIONIST IS BANK OFFICIAL

Col. William S. Barker

HUNTINGTON PARK, Oct. 8.—The City National Bank of this city now has another vice-president, Col. William S. Barker, for many years an outstanding figure in the Salvation Army and director of its overseas service during the World War, having been added to this list of officials at this bank. A substantial interest has been acquired in the bank by Col. Barker, according to Ralph Stephens, president of the bank.

Col. Barker entered the Salvation Army organization thirty-six years ago and continuously served that organization as a business executive until recent retirement from active duty. For many years he was secretary of the national organization and had charge of its real estate and legal departments throughout the United States. At the time of his retirement from active service in the army Col. Barker was vice-president of the Salvation Army corporation and chief executive officer in twelve Western States.

Anaheim Stages Annual Party

ANAHEIM, Oct. 8.—Anaheim’s sixth annual Halloween festival and parade will be held the evening of the 31st inst., it was decided by forty merchants at a dinner meeting in the Elks’ clubhouse last night.

Last year the Halloween fete attracted 35,000 persons to Anaheim.

In order to present a better attraction than those of past years committees will seek to present a better parade, it was decided. The street dance and other entertainment will be made secondary to the parade.

Fred Robins was named chairman of a committee to raise money for the event. The cost of presenting this fete was approximately $1000 last year, George W. Reid, secretary, announced.

As a special effort toward presenting a stronger parade feature, all communities of Orange county will be invited to send entries, and prizes more attractive than those usually posted will be offered, it was decided.

The speaker of the evening was Marc N. Goodnow, instructor in journalism at University of Southern California, who spoke on “Keeping Business at Home.”

WHITTIER BANKER IS HEART FAILURE VICTIM

WHITTIER, Oct. 8.—George J. Hazzard, 67 years of age, and for more than twenty-five years a resident of the Whittier district, died here today at his home, 648 East Turnbull Drive, from heart disease.

He had been prominent in the financial, social and civic affairs of the community. He was formerly president of the Home Savings Bank, and a director in the Whittier National Bank. He was at one time president of the Board of Trustees of the local high school, and was on the board continuously for twelve years.

He was born at Lansing, Mich. He leaves his widow, Mrs. Mary Hazzard, a daughter, Mrs. Greta Hazzard McLaren, and two sons, Carroll and Donald. Funeral services will be private at the home Thursday afternoon.

IMPERIAL ANNOUNCES WINTER FAIR

County Sponsors Unique Annual Event; to Build New Buildings

EL CENTRO, Oct. 8.—Imperial Valley’s Midwinter Fair is to be revived as a county project and the next exposition held in February, 1930, according to plans approved by the County Supervisors in session yesterday afternoon. President Andy Preble and members of the newly appointed board of fair directors appeared before the Supervisors with plans which they said received the approval of a large number of valley residents. They stated that they proposed to spend the major part of the $37,365 appropriation received from the county this year for the erection of grand-stand, administration and other buildings, modeled after those in the Los Angeles county fair grounds in Pomona.

The buildings are to be erected on an eighty-acre site adjoining the city of Imperial, which was purchased by the Supervisors for fair purposes four years ago. The Imperial Midwinter Fair formerly was sponsored by Brawley business men but was discontinued two years ago after two financially disastrous seasons.

It was explained by the fair directors that the selection of February dates this winter was agreed upon in order to allow time for the erection of buildings. These dates may be changed in the future, it was stated.

Grape Growers Are Victims of Drivers’ Strike

ONTARIO, Oct. 8.—Grape growers and shippers of this district are feeling the sting of the strike declared in New York by the truck drivers’ union. A great number of carloads of grapes sent to eastern terminals within the past week and days have become tied up in New York because of the truck drivers’ refusal to move the perishable crops.

The grapes were ready for consumption upon arrival at New York but being held over in the cars is causing them to rot into total loss, according to word received here by grape shippers and growers.

Many of the vineyards of the softsethn district, embracing most of Southern California growers, are losing heavily because of the action of the truck drivers in not moving the crops and not permitting commission men to remove them from the cars.

Recently the local grape men voted to curtail shipments approximately 50 per cent. Other markets have become glutted since the strike was called in New York and at present there is no eastern market for California grapes. Pleas made with the Interstate Commerce Commission have failed to bring relief to the grape men.

GLENDALE MAN BUSY WITH MONKEY BUSINESS

GLENDALE, Oct. 8.—F. M. Ayers, 306 North Highland avenue, is in the position of the man who grabbed a bear by the tail and then yelled for someone to help him let it go. A wandering monkey invaded Ayers’s garage early this morning and Ayers slammed the door on it. Then he called the police. Detective Sergeant Brown closed one eye and sighted through the garage doors with the other and declared that it seemed to be a perfectly good monkey, but as he hadn’t lost any simian pet he did not see what Ayers expected him to do about it.

Poundmaster Allen was next called and said he had no report of any missing monkey, and he also declined to tear any red tape in rounding up Ayers’s captive and disposing of it. Meantime Ayers has the monkey locked up in his garage, where it is juggling noisily with everything that is not nailed down, while Ayers regrets his obedience to the first impulse that led him to shut the beast up in his garage.

Giant Dirigible on Fire After Blast Falls Into River Near Hull, England, After Trial Flight Today.

LONDON, Aug. 24.—The new American dirigible ZR-2 was wrecked when it broke in two and exploded near Hull today.

Only two men out of more than 50 on board are known to have been saved.

More than 20 of those on board were Americans.

The two jumped from the blazing bag in parachutes and came down safely.

The machine was nearing the end of a trial flight which was to establish her fitness for a trans-Atlantic trip to America.

Going up into yesterday, the great machine worked perfectly, responding readily to the control levers and riding easily despite a high wind which was encountered.

While over Hull at 5:45 p. m. today shortly after she had signaled that she was going to make a test flight for speed, the huge gas bag exploded.

The dirigible broke in two and plunged into the river Humber.

The machine was carrying about 50 men. Some Britishers, under whose direction it had been built, others the Americans who were being trained in her management for the trip to the U. S.

There had been vague rumors that the airship was not behaving in an altogether satisfactory manner and that there were some defects in her fabric, but these reports were denied.

The trial trip on which the explosion occurred was begun after these reports had been circulated.

It was said that some of the metal framework was weakened and that she “humped” in the middle. It was said also that some reinforcements had to be made because of that defect.

75 ENTRIES FOR AUTO EXHIBIT

With more than 75 entries guaranteed, arrangements for the street decorations, music and entertainment complete, Anaheim’s first Midsummer Exhibit of the Orange County Auto Trades Assn. will open Friday noon and continue until 11 p. m.

Several thousand persons from surrounding ranches and neighboring towns are expected to be on hand for the event, and as an added inducement many merchants will hold a bedrock price sale.

There has probably never been an automobile show in the county where a larger and more complete variety of models handled in this county were on display. FORMER ANAHEIM PASTOR SUCCUMBS

Rev. Peter Stoetters, 63, chaplain of the Convent of Our Lady of Mercy, Los Angeles, died yesterday. Funeral services will be at 9:30 a. m. Friday at the Cathedral of St. Vibiana, and interment will be in Calvary cemetery, Los Angeles.

Father Stoetters entered this diocese as pastor of St. Boniface Catholic church, Anaheim, in 1886. Dispose of New Bungalow-ct and Complete Plans in Few Days for Erection of Another Court.

Ross Bros., of the Orange County Realty Co., have just completed a realty deal totaling $250,000, in which they have disposed of their new brick bungalow-ct on Clementine-st.

Plans will be completed in a few days for another bungalow-ct on a lot 146x165 just north of the court which has been sold. The new court will include eight four-room apartments, making it a little more that half as large as the one sold. The style of architecture will be similar.

It will face Chartres-st.

The new owner of the court which has been sold is Isaac N. Glover of Los Angeles, who disposed of a fine, full-bearing orange and walnut grove on the boulevard near Whittier.

His orange and walnut grove goes to J. G. Delozier who disposes to Ross Bros. one of the finest 100-acre ranches in the Imperial valley, on the boulevard near El Centro. It is highly improved with fine, two-story house, fences, etc. It has been considered one of the show ranches of the valley.

For their court, in addition to the ranch, Ross Bros. receive a considerable sum of money. The court, which brings in an income of $610 per month, was valued at $70,000 in the exchange.

Another deal was the sale of a ten-acre lemon and valencia grove at Yorba Linda by Frank Gauldin to Delor and Colvin who gave as part consideration a 160-acre ranch near Holtville in Imperial Valley. The balance was cash.

The sale of the court by Ross Bros. marks a total of more than $100,000 worth of apartments and residence property they have constructed and sold within the last year. Practically all the buildings material was purchased locally, the lumber from Gibson Lumber Co., plumbing from H. H. Garrison, electric wiring and fixtures from Holland Co., and Anaheim Electric Co. All the painting was done by Anaheim contractors.

This construction has made homes for 35 families who would otherwise have been unable to reside here.

J. R. Hamlin, with 20 years experience in building, a recent comer from Freeport, Ill., where he built most of the larger buildings, directed construction of the court. His work was considered so satisfactory that the Los Angeles Brick Co. sent representatives here to inspect it and recently a picture of the court was featured in an advertisement for the brick company was published in the Southwestern Contractor.

The brick company officials declare the court is the most up-to-date and well built of any they have seen in So. Calif.

KIDNAPER KILLED IN ESCAPE ATTEMPT

LOS ANGELES, Aug. 24.—A far-reaching investigation to determine how a number of hacksaws were smuggled into the jail and the manner in which the man escaped from his cell was ordered today by Sheriff Traeger as the result of the gun battle and killing of Horace Box, 27, former Long Beach fireman, when he attempted to escape from the county jail early today.

Box was discovered while cutting the bars of an outside jail window shortly after 2 a. m. by Deputy Sheriff Al Patton.

A terrific fight between Box and the deputy sheriff followed.

Box was wounded three times before a bullet from a revolver fired by Deputy Sheriff Cordon killed the escaping prisoner.

In the fight Deputy Patton was struck over the head with the heavy bar of a jail cot.

Box was being held for robbery and an attack upon Miss Lucille Urease of Long Beach several weeks ago.

BIG SPLENDID CHARITY BY CHICAGO NEWS

The Chicago Daily News deserves great credit for instituting and sustaining a charity that is novel and immensely useful—a fresh-air fund sanitarum for sick babies. This charity has just opened its 35th season in a new $271,000 fireproof building on an island in Lincoln Park, Chicago. This institution, since it was founded, has cared for more than 70,000 sick babies. Everything at the sanitarium is free, including medical treatment for children and for mothers if needed. The charity fund that maintains the institution is supported, as stated, by contributions ranging from 10 cents upward from over the city and county and from beyond the state.

Successful, cooperative publishers usually abstain from taking up, directly, activities which have no connection with the production of a newspaper. The old adage that the shoemaker should stick to his last, holds type of publishers’ regard any newspaper. The [illegible] newspaper’s field is the practical of directly assisting in activities outside of his journalistic sphere, either the newspaper or the outside enterprise would suffer therefrom. For the production of a first-class, successful newspaper is in itself such an exacting and complex work as admits of no distraction from it.

But this work of the Chicago Daily News is exceptional. It meets a manifest need of a great metropolitan city. It saves many an infantile life, and it stimulates public interest in philanthropies of this nature. Generally speaking, however, the newspaper best promotes activities of this kind, not by undertaking them itself, but by encouraging and supporting the work thru its columns.

AMERICA TO THE RESCUE FOR HUNGRY RUSSIA

America is going to the rescue of starving Russia, with the same zeal that it has shown in caring for the perishing in Belgium during its dark days, and for the children of Central and Southeastern Europe in more recent times. The American Flag, an emblem of mercy and generosity, as well as of justice, soon will be flying over food supply stations in Petrograd and Moscow. One million children will be fed by the American relief Organization and fully $10,000,000 worth of food—the gift of Americans—will be distributed among the famishing of Russia.

Of nothing have Americans greater reason to feel proud than of their generous and philanthropic impulses and the good things they do, prompt and by these impulses. From no part of the world does the cry of distress and appeal for aid come to America is not met with laden, unhearing ears. Americans respond swiftly and liberally, and their charitable sympathies go with their merciful ministrations.

HEROIC LIFE-SACRIFICE BY PASADENAN

August Kaufman, Pasadena cement contractor, made heroic sacrifice of his life for his children—sacrificed that was truly manly and noble. The story of his fruitless search for water for his wife and little ones has been published.

It develops that Kaufman, when he started on his search for water, took with him a small quantity of water and some oranges, to sustain him. But as he did not find any springs, and as he struggled with the desert and with thirst to get back to his loved ones, he would not take the water which he carried, even tho it might mean the saving of his life. He conserved it for his wife and children. And when his body was found, his untouched water and the uneaten oranges were found upon him.

This is heroism—simple, unostentatious, homely, but none the less heroism.

A born indeed, to humanity, will it be, if the confident claim of a Brooklyn eye specialist is fulfilled. He has evolved a serum which, it is asserted, will restore sight in cases of blindness caused by atrophy of the optic nerve, a condition which has been regarded as incurable. The formula for this serum soon is to be placed before the world by this specialist, who is responsible and who has high standing in his profession.

Science indeed has wrought marvels and continues working them. Many delicate operations are performed on eyes with remarkable results. Eye surgery has been developed amazingly. Let’s hope and pray that this discovery shall be the blessing that Dr. Ford expects it to be.

SAVAGE TIRES
HISTORY OF THE RED MAN SERIES

THE COUNCIL OF WAR
BY “INDIAN” MILLER

White men often ask why Indians wear long hair. There are many reasons; but I will tell a few. But first I would ask: Why should we cut the hair? God willed that men should grow long hair. The races that cut their hair are rapidly becoming baldheaded. Whoever saw a baldheaded Indian? Hair protects the head in many ways. The Indian who lives much in the open and in dry places keeps his face and lips from cracking by wrapping his hair around his face; and in the same way he protects his face from flying sand.

There are many other things we could say; but here is one reason more important than all. No Indian with short hair would have been admitted to a council of war. A council of war was a council of men; not of boys or women. It was considered a mark of cowardice for an Indian to cut his hair, for he thereby lowered the value of his scalp. Those Indians who braided their hair always braided a little scalp lock on the back of the head. This was for the convenience of the enemy in taking the scalp. It was already to tie to the bridle as an ornament.

What was the purpose of the council of war? It was to declare war or to plan a campaign. When war was declared the warriors put on warpaint. The warpaint was a sign of mourning as well as a sign of war; and it generally consisted of black alone.

It was customary for everyone to stand aside on the trail to allow one in mourning to pass; and a man was rash indeed who expected an Indian on the warpath to give half the trail. Indians on the warpath were allowed the whole trail. The council of war gave this authority.

In the wigwam of The Spreckels “Savage” Tire Company in the Fall of 1919 was held a Council of War. The decision to build a Cord tire was made. It was decided further that this tire must be a mighty tire—mightier than any that had ever been built before.

That tire—the Savage Cord—is now on the market. It is on the war path and claims the whole trail, for the company back of it has done everything within its power to make it the best tire ever produced—it is Built to Excel.
